I need to make a decision for the current Monopoly turn.

I have $324 and just passed GO. I built one house on Oriental Avenue. I hold a light blue monopoly with three houses on Vermont and Connecticut. Most other properties are mortgaged. I can build more houses or trade with players 1 and 2.

One more house on Vermont or Oriental is the only worthwhile upgrade. It costs $50 and raises the rent to $400. A second house would leave me with about $749, which p2 could then kill me on a 10. I will not build more, unmortgage, or trade. I will end my turn.

I realized St James Place is 16 spaces from GO, so p2 cannot reach it on a 10. The threat of landing there is only on my next turn, not before I can act again.

I am checking the exact positions from Reading Railroad. A roll of 11 lands on St James Place, where p2 holds three houses and the rent is $550. I need to confirm whether I can liquidate assets before paying rent during my next turn.

I now see that mortgage and sell actions may be available during debt resolution, not only after the turn ends. Without building a second house, my total liquidity is about $774. p2 can afford one more orange house for $100, so they will likely upgrade the property I am most likely to land on.

Only St James Place is reachable from Reading Railroad on the next roll, and only with a 11. Tennessee and New York are impossible. Dark blue properties are too far away. The other nearby spaces are mortgaged, so there is no immediate threat.

St James Place is the only reachable threat from Reading Railroad. A roll of 11 lands there for $550, which I can easily cover with my current liquidity. A fourth house would raise rent to $750, leaving me with only about $24 or bankrupting me at $749. I will not build that house.

I am weighing whether p2 will actually build a fourth house on St James. With $774 liquidity, the $750 rent would not bankrupt me, so they may not need to upgrade. I also considered the expected value of adding a second house to either Vermont or Connecticut, but Oriental is already fully upgraded.

The expected value of a fourth house on Vermont is only about $18, and on Connecticut about $17, both well below the $50 cost. The previous analysis that one fourth house is positive expected value applies to long-term survival, not this single roll.

The first house on Oriental was positive expected value because it raised liquidity to $774, safely above the $750 bankruptcy threshold. The second house would drop liquidity to $749, creating a real bankruptcy window if p2 builds a fourth house on St James and I roll a 11.

The exact turn order is now clear. I end my turn first, then p1 moves, then p2 rolls from GO. If p2 survives paying me and has cash left, they can build a fourth house before I roll again.

A roll of 11 lands on St James Place for $750. With $749 in liquidity, that would bankrupt me. The probability of rolling 11 is only about 5.6 percent. Because my liquidity is currently $774, p2 cannot kill me by building there, but the second house creates a kill condition that did not exist before.

The expected value of a fourth house on St James Place is only about eleven dollars for p2, well below the one hundred dollar cost. They might still build it to threaten player one or for future orbits. Player one is in jail and cannot reach orange soon.

Player one can escape jail by rolling doubles. A roll of six lands on St James Place for $550 or $750. A roll of eight lands on Tennessee for the same rent. New York is unreachable from jail.

Player one has a two-in-thirty-six chance of escaping jail by rolling doubles. If they land on orange with only thirty-eight dollars cash, they would need to sell houses to survive. Player one holds five houses across the red monopoly for three hundred seventy-five dollars in liquidation value. Combined with mortgageable properties worth four hundred eighty dollars and cash, total liquidity reaches eight hundred ninety-three dollars. This easily covers both five-hundred-fifty-dollar and seven-hundred-fifty-dollar rent.

Unmortgaging is not worthwhile. Mediterranean costs thirty-three dollars to unmortgage and offers no monopoly. Reading Railroad and Pennsy Railroad together cost two hundred twenty dollars, but the rent would only be fifty dollars.

I cannot trade away States Avenue to player two, because that would complete their pink monopoly. I will not unmortgage any properties.

I am now considering trading Ventnor Avenue. It would not complete a monopoly by itself, since neither player holds two yellows yet. Player one already has the red monopoly and Marvin Gardens, so I am looking for a trade that would either hurt player two or give me cash and monopolies.

Player two is the main threat. Their dark blue monopoly with houses is lethal if I land there, and their orange properties with three houses pay five hundred fifty to six hundred dollars in rent. Player two has one hundred thirty-four dollars cash and liquidation value of about six hundred fifty dollars from houses and utilities. My light blue monopoly with four houses can bankrupt anyone who lands there.

Player two cannot be bankrupted by my light blue houses. Their cash plus house equity and mortgages covers the $400 rent on Oriental and the $450 rent on Connecticut. Selling three orange houses would only raise about $150, which is still short. I will not build more houses.

Mortgaging would not help because the cash would be nearly identical and reversing it later costs ten percent interest. Player one is too weak to be useful in a trade. I am now considering whether player two might trade Pennsylvania Avenue to complete my green monopoly.

Completing the green monopoly would require unmortgaging Pacific and North Carolina and buying Pennsylvania Avenue, which costs more than my current cash. Even a bare green monopoly would pay only modest rent. Player two will not trade away their orange or dark blue properties. I will end my turn.

I will keep my public message brief and avoid revealing the fourth-house threat or liquidity calculations. I also notice the bank has only three houses left, so building two more would leave just one for player two to purchase.

I am now weighing a housing shortage strategy. Player two has three houses on each orange property and wants fourth houses. Buying two more now would leave only one house in the bank, blocking them from upgrading. The cost is one hundred dollars, leaving me with two hundred twenty-four dollars cash. Liquidity drops to seven hundred twenty-four dollars, which is still below the seven hundred fifty-dollar rent on St James Place if player two builds a fourth house there. I am deciding whether that risk is worth the strategic advantage.

Building both remaining houses leaves only one in the bank. Player two can still purchase exactly one fourth house, so they can still kill me on St James Place. My liquidity drops to seven hundred twenty-four dollars, which is below the seven hundred fifty-dollar rent threshold. Building more houses does not deny them the killing upgrade; it merely creates the kill condition. I will not build.
